plan.topic_summary: Large language model inference is shifting from a secondary workload to the dominant compute demand, driving new semiconductor architectures optimized for memory bandwidth, low-latency interconnect, and power efficiency. The question is how this shift reshapes the semiconductor value chain—memory, packaging, interconnect, and accelerator design—over a 1-to-5-year horizon.
key_questions: What is the current balance of inference versus training demand in hyperscaler and enterprise deployments, and how is this affecting accelerator mix and procurement priorities?
How are memory bandwidth and HBM supply constraints currently limiting inference throughput and cost per token, and what is the expected relief timeline?

What new inference-optimized architectures (chiplet designs, expanded on-package SRAM, CXL memory pooling) are reaching production in the next 1-3 years, and what performance-per-watt advantages do they offer over general-purpose GPUs?
How are interconnect standards (UALink, NVLink, PCIe Gen6) evolving to support multi-chip and multi-node inference at scale, and what are the adoption timelines?

Will inference workloads drive a fundamental shift in semiconductor packaging and memory hierarchy over 3-5 years, or will general-purpose accelerators with incremental memory upgrades remain sufficient?
What is the trajectory of inference cost per token, and at what point does this change the unit economics of AI deployment at scale for enterprises and cloud providers?

sources.title: FlashDecoding++: Faster Large Language Model Inference on GPUs
sources.abstract: As the Large Language Model (LLM) becomes increasingly important in various domains. However, the following challenges still remain unsolved in accelerating LLM inference: (1) Synchronized partial softmax update. The softmax operation requires a synchronized update operation among each partial softmax result, leading to ~20% overheads for the attention computation in LLMs. (2) Under-utilized computation of flat GEMM. The shape of matrices performing GEMM in LLM inference is flat, leading to under-utilized computation and >50% performance loss after padding zeros in previous designs. (3) Performance loss due to static dataflow. Kernel performance in LLM depends on varied input data features, hardware configurations, etc. A single and static dataflow may lead to a 50.25% performance loss for GEMMs of different shapes in LLM inference. We present FlashDecoding++, a fast LLM inference engine supporting mainstream LLMs and hardware back-ends. To tackle the above challenges, FlashDecoding++ creatively proposes: (1) Asynchronized softmax with unified max value. FlashDecoding++ introduces a unified max value technique for different partial softmax computations to avoid synchronization. (2) Flat GEMM optimization with double buffering. FlashDecoding++ points out that flat GEMMs with different shapes face varied bottlenecks. Then, techniques like double buffering are introduced. (3) Heuristic dataflow with hardware resource adaptation. FlashDecoding++ heuristically optimizes dataflow using different hardware resource considering input dynamics. Due to the versatility of optimizations in FlashDecoding++, FlashDecoding++ can achieve up to 4.86x and 2.18x speedup on both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs compared to Hugging Face implementations. FlashDecoding++ also achieves an average speedup of 1.37x compared to state-of-the-art LLM inference engines on mainstream LLMs.

sources.title: Profiling Large Language Model Inference on Apple Silicon: A Quantization Perspective
sources.abstract: A systematic understanding of Apple Silicon is lacking in the current landscape of hardware efficiency; research focus is largely centered on accelerating GPUs for large-scale training or inference on CUDA devices. This paper investigates Apple Silicon's unique memory architecture that offers a unified memory integrating CPU and GPU memory and its implications for on-device LLM inference. We decipher myths about whether Apple Silicon is efficient for on-device inference compared to competitors such as NVIDIA GPUs by directly conducting latency and throughput comparison benchmarks. We explain the performance gap between them through profiling low level hardware metrics - ALU utilization, memory bandwidth, buffer usage, cache residency etc. at runtime. We draw several insights regarding performance bottlenecks such as dequantization overhead, compute throughput and memory bandwidth. We debunk existing false claims regarding large language model inference such as compressing models to lower bit precision is a defacto promise for faster inference across all hardware platforms. We find that the large unified memory enables Apple Silicon to be both cost effective and efficient against NVIDIA GPUs for ultra large language models. Our large scale evaluation on 5 hardware testbeds incorporating three Apple M-series devices: M2 Ultra, M2 Max and M4 Pro and two NVIDIA GPUs: NVIDIA RTX A6000, a multi GPU setup with 2xNVIDIA RTX A6000, 5 model scales ranging from 8B to 405B parameters and 14 quantization schemes gives an understanding of how Apple Silicon fits within the paradigm of on-device LLM inference. Our analysis reveals multiple resource interdependencies and unexpected findings, while also quantifying established insights. To the best of our knowledge, this study makes the first attempt to present a thorough characterization and analysis of Apple Silicon for on-device inference.

sources.title: PowerInfer-2: Fast Large Language Model Inference on a Smartphone
sources.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) on smartphones enable real-time AI assistance and privacy-preserving, offline operation. However, resource constraints of smartphones limit current deployments to small language models (SLMs), significantly compromising their capabilities. This paper introduces PowerInfer-2, a smartphone-based framework that enables fast inference for LLMs exceeding the memory capacity. The key insight is decomposing matrix operations into neuron clusters as the basic processing unit, which enables flexible scheduling and efficient I/O-computation pipelining. PowerInfer-2 leverages this neuron-cluster-based design in both computation and storage. For computation, neuron clusters with dense activations are processed on NPU, while sparse clusters use CPU. The storage engine provides a fine-grained pipeline mechanism that coordinates cluster-level computation and I/O operations, enhanced by a segmented neuron cache to reduce I/O activities. PowerInfer-2 achieves up to a 27.8x speed increase compared to state-of-the-art frameworks. PowerInfer-2 is the first system to serve a 47B LLM on a smartphone, achieving 11.68 tokens/s. Notably, these performance improvements preserve model quality with negligible accuracy degradation.

sources.title: Accelerating Large Language Model Inference via Early-Exiting Algorithms
sources.abstract: Large language models have achieved remarkable capabilities, but their practical deployment is hindered by significant computational costs. While adaptive computation methods like early-exiting promise to reduce these costs, they introduce a fundamental conflict: the per-token dynamism intended to save computation often creates system-level bottlenecks that can paradoxically reduce throughput in batched inference. This dissertation resolves this conflict by co-designing adaptive algorithms and model architectures to strike an optimal balance between dynamism and efficiency. To this end, our work first addresses critical sources of overhead in conventional early-exiting by proposing an efficient parallel decoding mechanism. We then show that deep parameter sharing provides an architectural foundation that not only yields compact, parameter-efficient models but also inherently mitigates the critical synchronization issues affecting dynamic inference. Finally, this work presents a unified framework where lightweight routers are pretrained to dynamically assign an optimal recursion depth for each token. This approach establishes a new Pareto frontier between efficiency and performance by effectively optimizing for both adaptive computation and parameter efficiency within a single model.

sources.title: Large Language Model Inference Acceleration: A Comprehensive Hardware Perspective
sources.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across various fields, from natural language understanding to text generation. Compared to non-generative LLMs like BERT and DeBERTa, generative LLMs like GPT series and Llama series are currently the main focus due to their superior algorithmic performance. The advancements in generative LLMs are closely intertwined with the development of hardware capabilities. Various hardware platforms exhibit distinct hardware characteristics, which can help improve LLM inference performance. Therefore, this paper comprehensively surveys efficient generative LLM inference on different hardware platforms. First, we provide an overview of the algorithm architecture of mainstream generative LLMs and delve into the inference process. Then, we summarize different optimization methods for different platforms such as CPU, GPU, FPGA, ASIC, and PIM/NDP, and provide inference results for generative LLMs. Furthermore, we perform a qualitative and quantitative comparison of inference performance with batch sizes 1 and 8 on different hardware platforms by considering hardware power consumption, absolute inference speed (tokens/s), and energy efficiency (tokens/J). We compare the performance of the same optimization methods across different hardware platforms, the performance across different hardware platforms, and the performance of different methods on the same hardware platform. This provides a systematic and comprehensive summary of existing inference acceleration work by integrating software optimization methods and hardware platforms. We point out that three trends (multimodality, inference-time compute, and higher inference energy efficiency) are promising to redefine the capabilities of edge artificial intelligence systems. Our project is available at https://dai.sjtu.edu.cn/project.html.

sources.title: Accelerating Large Language Model Inference with Self-Supervised Early Exits
sources.abstract: This paper presents a modular approach to accelerate inference in large language models (LLMs) by adding early exit heads at intermediate transformer layers. Each head is trained in a self-supervised manner to mimic the main model's predictions, allowing computation to stop early when a calibrated confidence threshold is reached. We evaluate several confidence metrics and show that entropy provides the most reliable separation between correct and incorrect predictions. Experiments on the Pythia model suite (70M to 2.8B parameters) demonstrate that our method significantly reduces inference cost while maintaining accuracy across multiple benchmarks. We further adapt this approach to speculative decoding, introducing Dynamic Self-Speculative Decoding (DSSD), which achieves 1.66x higher token acceptance than manually-tuned LayerSkip baselines with minimal hyperparameter tuning.

sources.title: LLMCompass: Enabling Efficient Hardware Design for Large Language Model Inference
sources.venue: Proceedings - International Symposium on Computer Architecture/Proceedings
sources.abstract: The past year has witnessed the increasing popularity of Large Language Models (LLMs). Their unprecedented scale and associated high hardware cost have impeded their broader adoption, calling for efficient hardware designs. With the large hardware needed to simply run LLM inference, evaluating different hardware designs becomes a new bottleneck. This work introduces LLMCompass1, a hardware evaluation framework for LLM inference workloads. LLMCompass is fast, accurate, versatile, and able to describe and evaluate different hardware designs. LLMCompass includes a mapper to automatically find performance-optimal mapping and scheduling. It also incorporates an area-based cost model to help architects reason about their design choices. Compared to real-world hardware, LLMCompass’ estimated latency achieves an average $10.9\%$ error rate across various operators with various input sizes and an average $4.1\%$ error rate for LLM inference. With LLMCompass, simulating a 4-NVIDIA A100 GPU node running GPT-3 175B inference can be done within 16 minutes on commodity hardware, including 26,400 rounds of the mapper’s parameter search. With the aid of LLMCompass, this work draws architectural implications and explores new cost-effective hardware designs. By reducing the compute capability or replacing High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) with traditional DRAM, these new designs can achieve as much as 3.41x improvement in performance/cost compared to an NVIDIA A100, making them promising choices for democratizing LLMs.1Available at https://github.com/PrincetonUniversity/LLMCompass.

sources.title: Self-Selected Attention Span for Accelerating Large Language Model Inference
sources.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can solve challenging tasks. However, their inference computation on modern GPUs is highly inefficient due to the increasing number of tokens they must attend to as they generate new ones. To address this inefficiency, we capitalize on LLMs' problem-solving capabilities to optimize their own inference-time efficiency. We demonstrate with two specific tasks: (a) evaluating complex arithmetic expressions and (b) summarizing news articles. For both tasks, we create custom datasets to fine-tune an LLM. The goal of fine-tuning is twofold: first, to make the LLM learn to solve the evaluation or summarization task, and second, to train it to identify the minimal attention spans required for each step of the task. As a result, the fine-tuned model is able to convert these self-identified minimal attention spans into sparse attention masks on-the-fly during inference. We develop a custom CUDA kernel to take advantage of the reduced context to attend to. We demonstrate that using this custom CUDA kernel improves the throughput of LLM inference by 28%. Our work presents an end-to-end demonstration showing that training LLMs to self-select their attention spans speeds up autoregressive inference in solving real-world tasks.

sources.title: FlightLLM: Efficient Large Language Model Inference with a Complete Mapping Flow on FPGAs
sources.venue: ACM/SIGDA International Symposium on Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGA)
sources.abstract: Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) have made a significant impact on various domains. However, LLMs' efficiency suffers from both heavy computation and memory overheads. Compression techniques like sparsification and quantization are commonly used to mitigate the gap between LLM's computation/memory overheads and hardware capacity. However, existing GPU and transformer-based accelerators cannot efficiently process compressed LLMs, due to the following unresolved challenges: low computational efficiency, underutilized memory bandwidth, and large compilation overheads. This paper proposes FlightLLM, enabling efficient LLMs inference with a complete mapping flow on FPGAs. In FlightLLM, we highlight an innovative solution that the computation and memory overhead of LLMs can be solved by utilizing FPGA-specific resources (e.g., DSP48 and heterogeneous memory hierarchy). We propose a configurable sparse DSP chain to support different sparsity patterns with high computation efficiency. Second, we propose an always-on-chip decode scheme to boost memory bandwidth with mixed-precision support. Finally, to make FlightLLM available for real-world LLMs, we propose a length adaptive compilation method to reduce the compilation overhead. Implemented on the Xilinx Alveo U280 FPGA, FlightLLM achieves 6.0× higher energy efficiency and 1.8× better cost efficiency against commercial GPUs (e.g., NVIDIA V100S) on modern LLMs (e.g., LLaMA2-7B) using vLLM and SmoothQuant under the batch size of one. FlightLLM beats NVIDIA A100 GPU with 1.2× higher throughput using the latest Versal VHK158 FPGA.

sources.title: Structural Embedding Projection for Contextual Large Language Model Inference
sources.abstract: Structured embedding transformations offer a promising approach for enhancing the efficiency and coherence of language model inference. The introduction of Structural Embedding Projection (SEP) provides a mechanism for refining token representations through projection matrices that integrate hierarchical and relational dependencies. The mathematical formulation of SEP enables embedding spaces to capture structured contextual relationships, thereby improving semantic fidelity without significantly increasing computational overhead. Experimental evaluations conducted on a range of linguistic datasets revealed that SEP contributed to reductions in perplexity and enhanced contextual coherence, demonstrating its potential to refine language model outputs. Computational efficiency assessments highlighted variations across different datasets, suggesting that the integration of structured embeddings introduced dataset-dependent trade-offs between inference speed and representational richness. The qualitative analysis of generated responses indicated that SEP enhanced narrative consistency and topic alignment, leading to improved fluency in multi-sentence text generation. The modifications to embedding layers required precise optimization to ensure stable training dynamics, as the introduction of structured transformations altered the traditional representation-learning process. The architectural adjustments necessary for SEP implementation influenced inference latency and memory consumption, requiring a balance between efficiency gains and additional processing demands. The impact of SEP on lexical diversity suggested that embedding modifications influenced the model's vocabulary usage, reflecting a more context-aware selection of generated tokens.

sources.title: From Words to Watts: Benchmarking the Energy Costs of Large Language Model Inference
sources.venue: IEEE High Performance Extreme Computing Conference
sources.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have exploded in popularity due to their new generative capabilities that go far beyond prior state-of-the-art. These technologies are increasingly being leveraged in various domains such as law, finance, and medicine. However, these models carry significant computational challenges, especially the compute and energy costs required for inference. Inference energy costs already receive less attention than the energy costs of training LLMs-despite how often these large models are called on to conduct inference in reality (e.g., ChatGPT). As these state-of-the-art LLMs see increasing usage and deployment in various domains, a better understanding of their resource utilization is crucial for cost-savings, scaling performance, efficient hardware usage, and optimal inference strategies. In this paper, we describe experiments conducted to study the computational and energy utilization of inference with LLMs. We benchmark and conduct a preliminary analysis of the inference performance and inference energy costs of different sizes of LLaMA-a recent state-of-the-art LLM-developed by Meta AI on two generations of popular GPUs (NVIDIA V100 & A100) and two datasets (Alpaca and GSM8K) to reflect the diverse set of tasks/benchmarks for LLMs in research and practice. We present the results of multi-node, multi-GPU inference using model sharding across up to 32 GPUs. To our knowledge, our work is the one of the first to study LLM inference performance from the perspective of computational and energy resources at this scale.

sources.title: Energy Considerations of Large Language Model Inference and Efficiency Optimizations
sources.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) scale in size and adoption, their computational and environmental costs continue to rise. Prior benchmarking efforts have primarily focused on latency reduction in idealized settings, often overlooking the diverse real-world inference workloads that shape energy use. In this work, we systematically analyze the energy implications of common inference efficiency optimizations across diverse Natural Language Processing (NLP) and generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) workloads, including conversational AI and code generation. We introduce a modeling approach that approximates real-world LLM workflows through a binning strategy for input-output token distributions and batch size variations. Our empirical analysis spans software frameworks, decoding strategies, GPU architectures, online and offline serving settings, and model parallelism configurations. We show that the effectiveness of inference optimizations is highly sensitive to workload geometry, software stack, and hardware accelerators, demonstrating that naive energy estimates based on FLOPs or theoretical GPU utilization significantly underestimate real-world energy consumption. Our findings reveal that the proper application of relevant inference efficiency optimizations can reduce total energy use by up to 73% from unoptimized baselines. These insights provide a foundation for sustainable LLM deployment and inform energy-efficient design strategies for future AI infrastructure.

Performance figures (speedups, tokens/s, energy reductions) are self-reported by each system's own authors and were not independently replicated or cross-checked here.

sources.title: Splitwise: Efficient Generative LLM Inference Using Phase Splitting
sources.venue: Proceedings - International Symposium on Computer Architecture/Proceedings
sources.abstract: Generative large language model (LLM) applications are growing rapidly, leading to large-scale deployments of expensive and power-hungry GPUs. Our characterization of LLM inference shows that each inference request undergoes two phases: a compute-intensive prompt computation phase and a memory intensive token generation phase, each with distinct latency, throughput, memory, and power characteristics. Despite state-of-the-art batching and scheduling, the token generation phase underutilizes compute resources. Unlike prompt computation, token generation does not need the compute capability of the latest GPUs and can be run with lower power and cost. Based on these insights, we propose Splitwise, a model deployment and scheduling technique that splits the two phases of LLM inference requests on to separate machines. Splitwise enables phase-specific resource management using hardware that is well suited for each phase. Request state is transferred efficiently between machines using optimized network libraries on the fast back-plane interconnects available in today’s GPU clusters. Using Splitwise, we design homogeneous and heterogeneous LLM inference clusters optimized for throughput, cost, and power Compared to current designs, Splitwise clusters achieve up to $1.4 \times$ higher throughput at $\mathbf{2 0 \%}$ lower cost. Alternatively, they can deliver $2.35 \times$ more throughput under the same power and cost budgets.

sources.title: TokenPowerBench: Benchmarking the Power Consumption of LLM Inference
sources.abstract: Large language model (LLM) services now answer billions of queries per day, and industry reports show that inference, not training, accounts for more than 90% of total power consumption. However, existing benchmarks focus on either training/fine-tuning or performance of inference and provide little support for power consumption measurement and analysis of inference. We introduce TokenPowerBench, the first lightweight and extensible benchmark designed for LLM-inference power consumption studies. The benchmark combines (i) a declarative configuration interface covering model choice, prompt set, and inference engine, (ii) a measurement layer that captures GPU-, node-, and system-level power without specialized power meters, and (iii) a phase-aligned metrics pipeline that attributes energy to the prefill and decode stages of every request. These elements make it straight-forward to explore the power consumed by an LLM inference run; furthermore, by varying batch size, context length, parallelism strategy and quantization, users can quickly assess how each setting affects joules per token and other energy-efficiency metrics. We evaluate TokenPowerBench on four of the most widely used model series (Llama, Falcon, Qwen, and Mistral). Our experiments cover from 1 billion parameters up to the frontier-scale Llama3-405B model. Furthermore, we release TokenPowerBench as open source to help users to measure power consumption, forecast operating expenses, and meet sustainability targets when deploying LLM services.

sources.title: Towards Greener LLMs: Bringing Energy-Efficiency to the Forefront of LLM Inference
sources.abstract: With the ubiquitous use of modern large language models (LLMs) across industries, the inference serving for these models is ever expanding. Given the high compute and memory requirements of modern LLMs, more and more top-of-the-line GPUs are being deployed to serve these models. Energy availability has come to the forefront as the biggest challenge for data center expansion to serve these models. In this paper, we present the trade-offs brought up by making energy efficiency the primary goal of LLM serving under performance SLOs. We show that depending on the inputs, the model, and the service-level agreements, there are several knobs available to the LLM inference provider to use for being energy efficient. We characterize the impact of these knobs on the latency, throughput, as well as the energy. By exploring these trade-offs, we offer valuable insights into optimizing energy usage without compromising on performance, thereby paving the way for sustainable and cost-effective LLM deployment in data center environments.

sources.title: ShuffleInfer: Disaggregate LLM Inference for Mixed Downstream Workloads
sources.venue: ACM Transactions on Architecture and Code Optimization
sources.abstract: Transformer-based large language model (LLM) inference serving is now the backbone of many cloud services. LLM inference consists of a prefill phase and a decode phase. However, existing LLM deployment practices often overlook the distinct characteristics of these phases, leading to significant interference. To mitigate interference, our insight is to carefully schedule and group inference requests based on their characteristics. We realize this idea in ShuffleInfer through three pillars. First, it partitions prompts into fixed-size chunks so that the accelerator always runs close to its computation-saturated limit. Second, it disaggregates prefill and decode instances so each can run independently. Finally, it uses a smart two-level scheduling algorithm augmented with predicted resource usage to avoid decode scheduling hotspots. Results show that ShuffleInfer improves time-to-first-token (TTFT), job completion time (JCT), and inference efficiency in terms of performance per dollar by a large margin, e.g., it uses 38% less resources all the while lowering average TTFT and average JCT by 97% and 47%, respectively.

sources.title: CIMERA: Compute-in-Interconnect and Memory with Reconfigurable Precision for LLM Inference
sources.abstract: LLM impose significant computational and memory demands, creating challenges for energy-efficient inference across platforms ranging from data centers to power-constrained edge devices. Weight precision plays a critical role in balancing inference accuracy, throughput, and energy consumption, while modern LLM workloads exhibit pronounced heterogeneity and tolerance that favors adaptive precision execution. This paper presents CIMERA, a reconfigurable-precision LLM inference accelerator that integrates compute-in-interconnect and memory to mitigate the memory wall and enable precision-aware execution. Compared to Nvidia H100, CIMERA delivers up to $25\times$ and $10\times$ higher energy efficiency for 1B and 13B models, respectively.

sources.title: LLM-Inference-Bench: Inference Benchmarking of Large Language Models on AI Accelerators
sources.venue: International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking, Storage and Analysis (SC)
sources.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have propelled groundbreaking advancements across several domains and are commonly used for text generation applications. However, the computational demands of these complex models pose significant challenges, requiring efficient hardware acceleration. Benchmarking the performance of LLMs across diverse hardware platforms is crucial to understanding their scalability and throughput characteristics. We introduce LLM-Inference-Bench, a comprehensive benchmarking suite to evaluate the hardware inference performance of LLMs. We thoroughly analyze diverse hardware platforms, including GPUs from Nvidia and AMD and specialized AI accelerators, Intel Habana and SambaNova. Our evaluation includes several LLM inference frameworks and models from LLaMA, Mistral, and Qwen families with 7B and 70B parameters. Our benchmarking results reveal the strengths and limitations of various models, hardware platforms, and inference frameworks. We provide an interactive dashboard to help identify configurations for optimal performance for a given hardware platform.

sources.title: WattGPU: Predicting Inference Power and Latency on Unseen GPUs and LLMs
sources.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) inference workloads are a rapidly growing contributor to data center energy consumption. Optimizing these deployments requires matching specific LLMs to the most efficient GPUs, but operators currently lack the tools to do so without exhaustively profiling each combination. While some predictive models exist, they still require profiling data and struggle to generalize to hardware unseen during training. To address this, we introduce \textit{WattGPU}, featuring two predictive models for mean GPU power draw and Inter-Token Latency (ITL). Our approach leverages only publicly available LLM metadata and GPU specifications, eliminating the need for hardware access or profiling while enabling generalization to unseen NVIDIA server-grade GPUs and LLMs. We evaluate our models using rigorous leave-one-GPU-out and leave-one-LLM-out cross-validation on a dataset of 42 open-source LLMs (0.1B--27B parameters) and 8 GPUs under both offline and server scenarios. The mean power draw model achieves a median absolute percentage error of $\leq3.4\%$ for offline and $\leq13.5\%$ for server scenarios on unseen GPUs, while the latency model achieves $\leq8.5\%$ in server mode, both maintaining strong GPU ranking correlations for server scenarios (Kendall $τ\geq0.76$). Compared to standard physically grounded baselines -- Load-Scaled Thermal Design Power (TDP) for power draw and roofline for latency -- our models reduce median absolute percentage error by approximately 4$\times$ on unseen LLM-GPU combinations for server scenarios or approximately 2$\times$ for completely unseen GPUs. WattGPU's data and code are publicly available at https://github.com/maufadel/wattgpu.

sources.title: GEAR: An Efficient KV Cache Compression Recipe for Near-Lossless Generative Inference of LLM
sources.abstract: Key-value (KV) caching has become the de-facto to accelerate generation speed for large language models (LLMs) inference. However, the growing cache demand with increasing sequence length has transformed LLM inference to be a memory bound problem, significantly constraining the system throughput. Existing methods rely on dropping unimportant tokens or quantizing all entries uniformly. Such methods, however, often incur high approximation errors to represent the compressed matrices. The autoregressive decoding process further compounds the error of each step, resulting in critical deviation in model generation and deterioration of performance. To tackle this challenge, we propose GEAR, an efficient KV cache compression framework that achieves near-lossless high-ratio compression. GEAR first applies quantization to majority of entries of similar magnitudes to ultra-low precision. It then employs a low rank matrix to approximate the quantization error, and a sparse matrix to remedy individual errors from outlier entries. By adeptly integrating three techniques, GEAR is able to fully exploit their synergistic potentials. Our experiments demonstrate that compared to alternatives, GEAR achieves near-lossless 4-bit KV cache compression with up to 2.38x throughput improvement, while reducing peak-memory size up to 2.29x. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/HaoKang-Timmy/GEAR.

sources.title: Pie: Pooling CPU Memory for LLM Inference
sources.abstract: The rapid growth of LLMs has revolutionized natural language processing and AI analysis, but their increasing size and memory demands present significant challenges. A common solution is to spill over to CPU memory; however, traditional GPU-CPU memory swapping often results in higher latency and lower throughput. This paper introduces Pie, an LLM inference framework that addresses these challenges with performance-transparent swapping and adaptive expansion. By leveraging predictable memory access patterns and the high bandwidth of modern hardware like the NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper Superchip, Pie enables concurrent data swapping without affecting foreground computation, expanding effective memory without added latency. Adaptive expansion dynamically adjusts CPU memory allocation based on real-time information, optimizing memory usage and performance under varying conditions. Pie maintains low computation latency, high throughput, and high elasticity. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates that Pie achieves optimal swapping policy during cache warmup and effectively balances increased memory capacity with negligible impact on computation. With its extended capacity, Pie outperforms vLLM by up to 1.9X in throughput and 2X in latency. Additionally, Pie can reduce GPU memory usage by up to 1.67X while maintaining the same performance. Compared to FlexGen, an offline profiling-based swapping solution, Pie achieves magnitudes lower latency and 9.4X higher throughput.

sources.title: LLM Inference Unveiled: Survey and Roofline Model Insights
sources.abstract: The field of efficient Large Language Model (LLM) inference is rapidly evolving, presenting a unique blend of opportunities and challenges. Although the field has expanded and is vibrant, there hasn't been a concise framework that analyzes the various methods of LLM Inference to provide a clear understanding of this domain. Our survey stands out from traditional literature reviews by not only summarizing the current state of research but also by introducing a framework based on roofline model for systematic analysis of LLM inference techniques. This framework identifies the bottlenecks when deploying LLMs on hardware devices and provides a clear understanding of practical problems, such as why LLMs are memory-bound, how much memory and computation they need, and how to choose the right hardware. We systematically collate the latest advancements in efficient LLM inference, covering crucial areas such as model compression (e.g., Knowledge Distillation and Quantization), algorithm improvements (e.g., Early Exit and Mixture-of-Expert), and both hardware and system-level enhancements. Our survey stands out by analyzing these methods with roofline model, helping us understand their impact on memory access and computation. This distinctive approach not only showcases the current research landscape but also delivers valuable insights for practical implementation, positioning our work as an indispensable resource for researchers new to the field as well as for those seeking to deepen their understanding of efficient LLM deployment. The analyze tool, LLM-Viewer, is open-sourced.

sources.title: Break the Sequential Dependency of LLM Inference Using Lookahead Decoding
sources.abstract: Autoregressive decoding of large language models (LLMs) is memory bandwidth bounded, resulting in high latency and significant wastes of the parallel processing power of modern accelerators. Existing methods for accelerating LLM decoding often require a draft model (e.g., speculative decoding), which is nontrivial to obtain and unable to generalize. In this paper, we introduce Lookahead decoding, an exact, parallel decoding algorithm that accelerates LLM decoding without needing auxiliary models or data stores. It allows trading per-step log(FLOPs) to reduce the number of total decoding steps, is more parallelizable on single or multiple modern accelerators, and is compatible with concurrent memory-efficient attention (e.g., FlashAttention). Our implementation of Lookahead decoding can speed up autoregressive decoding by up to 1.8x on MT-bench and 4x with strong scaling on multiple GPUs in code completion tasks. Our code is avialable at https://github.com/hao-ai-lab/LookaheadDecoding

sources.title: Beyond the Chip: HBM, Advanced Packaging, and the Hidden Bottlenecks of Frontier AI:
sources.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
sources.abstract: Frontier AI supply-chain analysis often focuses on the most visible bottlenecks: leading-edge fabs, advanced lithography, and GPUs. But as AI accelerators become more powerful, the constraint may increasingly sit further upstream, in the technologies that allow those chips to work as high-performance systems. High-bandwidth memory (HBM) and advanced packaging are two such points of vulnerability. Research on HBM, chiplet interconnects, thermal management, and heterogeneous integration shows that these technologies face significant performance, reliability, manufacturing, and scaling constraints. This paper asks what would happen if HBM or advanced packaging became a binding constraint on frontier AI chip production, and which actors would have the greatest ability to reduce that vulnerability. I argue that strategic leverage should be assessed not only by market share, but by four characteristics: concentration, replaceability, the time required to expand capacity, and dependence between supply-chain nodes.

findings.claim: Energy availability is described as the largest constraint on expanding data centers for LLM serving, so inference growth may be limited by power rather than by chip supply or algorithms alone.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: src_ad2da04a95 is an arXiv preprint and has not been peer reviewed. src_c153ee89bf (Splitwise, peer-reviewed ISCA) also frames the problem as large deployments of expensive, power-hungry GPUs. Both abstracts describe the constraint but do not quantify how binding it is.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Energy availability has come to the forefront as the biggest challenge for data center expansion to serve these models.

findings.claim: Autoregressive decoding is memory-bandwidth bound and leaves accelerator compute idle. The bottleneck is structural, and software fixes only partly work around it.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: Three abstracts agree on memory-bound decoding. src_e77df27540 and src_d13d8443ba are arXiv preprints. The reported lookahead speedups (up to 1.8x on MT-bench, 4x with multi-GPU strong scaling on code completion) are task-specific and are not a general fix. The abstracts do not show how the gains hold across workloads or at production scale.
findings.supporting_excerpt: Autoregressive decoding of large language models (LLMs) is memory bandwidth bounded, resulting in high latency and significant wastes of the parallel processing power of modern accelerators.

findings.claim: HBM and advanced packaging are argued to be potential single points of failure for AI accelerator supply. Inference capacity could be limited by these upstream components rather than by GPUs or fabs.
findings.label: verified_fact
findings.rationale: This is a single Zenodo preprint (not peer reviewed) and a position paper. The abstract says the constraint 'may' sit upstream and poses a hypothetical about HBM or packaging becoming binding. It does not show that such a shortage has happened or give capacity numbers. Treat it as a risk hypothesis, not demonstrated evidence.
findings.supporting_excerpt: these technologies face significant performance, reliability, manufacturing, and scaling constraints.

findings.claim: KV-cache compression and quantization trade quality for memory and throughput. Errors compound across autoregressive steps, and the 'near-lossless' result is self-reported on the authors' own evaluation.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: The GEAR abstract (arXiv preprint) says existing methods incur high approximation errors that compound during decoding. GEAR itself claims near-lossless 4-bit compression with up to 2.38x throughput and 2.29x lower peak memory. The abstract does not state the models, tasks or sequence lengths used, so it is unclear whether near-lossless holds on long-context, reasoning or safety-sensitive tasks. This is a coverage gap, not evidence of failure.

findings.claim: Headline efficiency gains for inference systems come from different baselines, models and hardware, so they cannot be compared or added together. Many are 'up to' figures from the authors' own setups.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Splitwise reports up to 1.4x throughput at 20% lower cost. ShuffleInfer reports 38% fewer resources. Pie reports up to 1.9x over vLLM. CIMERA reports up to 25x energy efficiency versus H100 for a 1B model, falling to 10x for 13B. The efficiency advantage shrinks as model size grows, and the abstract does not say whether CIMERA was built in silicon or simulated. CIMERA and Pie are arXiv preprints. CIMERA has 0 citations and no independent replication is visible.

findings.claim: Several proposed optimizations depend on specific hardware or fast interconnects, which limits portability and adds vendor dependence and scheduling complexity.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: Splitwise relies on fast back-plane interconnects in current GPU clusters to move request state. Pie leans on the high bandwidth of the NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper Superchip. ShuffleInfer needs a two-level scheduler with predicted resource usage to avoid decode hotspots, which adds moving parts. The abstracts do not report results on slower interconnects or other vendors' hardware. Pie is a preprint.

findings.claim: Tools for measuring and predicting inference power are immature. Prediction errors are non-trivial in server settings, and the models and GPUs covered are narrow.
findings.label: ai_interpretation
findings.rationale: TokenPowerBench says existing benchmarks give little support for inference power measurement. WattGPU reports median error up to 13.5% for server-scenario power on unseen GPUs. Its data cover 42 open models up to 27B parameters on 8 NVIDIA server GPUs, so frontier-scale models and non-NVIDIA hardware are not covered. LLM-Inference-Bench tests only 7B and 70B models. All three are preprints or benchmark papers whose results the abstracts do not show to be independently reproduced.

findings.claim: The claim that inference accounts for more than 90% of total AI power consumption is attributed to unnamed 'industry reports'. It is not independently supported in the provided papers.
findings.label: unverified_claim
findings.rationale: The statement appears in the TokenPowerBench abstract (arXiv preprint) as background citing industry reports. No source, method or scope is given, and the other papers do not corroborate the figure. Training-versus-inference energy shares also likely vary by operator and period.

hype_flags: 'Up to 25x' energy efficiency vs H100 (CIMERA): a best-case figure for a 1B model that falls to 10x at 13B. It is an uncited-by-others preprint and the abstract does not state whether it was built or simulated.
'Near-lossless' KV-cache compression: this is the authors' own characterization, and the abstract does not say which tasks and context lengths were tested.
'Break the Sequential Dependency' (lookahead decoding): the framing overstates what the abstract reports, which is up to 1.8x on MT-bench and 4x only with multi-GPU scaling on code completion.
'Inference accounts for more than 90% of power': an unsourced industry-report figure repeated as background.
'Up to' throughput and cost claims (Splitwise, ShuffleInfer, Pie): these are best-case results against chosen baselines, not typical production outcomes.
HBM and packaging as the 'hidden bottleneck': this rests on a single non-peer-reviewed argument paper, and the abstract describes a hypothetical shortage, not an observed one.

finding.claim: S3 reports FlightLLM's 6.0x energy and 1.8x cost advantage as general 'commercial GPU' evidence. The abstract's comparison is against an older NVIDIA V100S, on LLaMA2-7B only, using vLLM and SmoothQuant baselines under a batch setting that the truncated abstract does not fully show. The result is self-reported by the FPGA authors. It does not show that FPGAs beat current-generation GPUs.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The baseline is a previous-generation GPU and a single 7B model. The abstract is cut off before the batch-size condition, so the scope of the result is unclear. S3 omits these limits. CIMERA's H100 comparison in a different paper is not comparable.
finding.supporting_excerpt: FlightLLM achieves 6.0× higher energy efficiency and 1.8× better cost efficiency against commercial GPUs (e.g., NVIDIA V100S) on modern LLMs (e.g., LLaMA2-7B)
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S5 says LLMCompass reports 'low error'. The abstract gives a 10.9% average error at operator level and 4.1% for LLM inference. That is not obviously low for design-space exploration. These errors are measured on existing hardware, whereas the headline 3.41x performance/cost gain comes from simulated designs that were never built.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: Validation error on A100-class systems does not carry over to novel architectures such as HBM-free designs. The 'as much as 3.41x' gain is a simulation result that should be flagged as unvalidated in silicon.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Compared to real-world hardware, LLMCompass’ estimated latency achieves an average $10.9\%$ error rate across various operators with various input sizes and an average $4.1\%$ error rate for LLM inference.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S6 is rated high-confidence and 'verified' but rests on a single source. The tension between per-token dynamism and batched throughput is stated in the dissertation abstract (src_a8b6fbc5ed). The second cited paper (src_911f9e6d7d) does not mention synchronization or batched-throughput problems in its abstract. That abstract reports early exits as working, and the dissertation itself claims to resolve the conflict. S6 therefore overstates how much independent support the tension has.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: Only the dissertation framing supports the tension claim, and the abstract gives no measured evidence for it. Citing the self-supervised early-exit paper for it is not supported by its abstract. Confidence should be medium at most.

finding.claim: S7 omits that the self-supervised early-exit results come only from small Pythia models (70M–2.8B parameters). The 1.66x figure is higher token acceptance relative to LayerSkip, not measured end-to-end speedup. Generalization to frontier-scale or batched serving is not shown. S6 itself flags batching problems for early exit.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: Token acceptance is a proxy metric. The study is a single preprint on small models with no peer review indicated.
finding.supporting_excerpt: Experiments on the Pythia model suite (70M to 2.8B parameters) demonstrate that our method significantly reduces inference cost while maintaining accuracy across multiple benchmarks.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S8 presents the self-selected attention span method as improving end-to-end autoregressive throughput without saying how narrow the evidence is. The abstract reports a 28% throughput gain on only two tasks (arithmetic expression evaluation and news summarization), using custom datasets and task-specific fine-tuning. It is not a general inference accelerator.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The model must be fine-tuned per task to learn spans. The gain is measured on authors' own tasks and datasets, so transfer to general workloads is unestablished.
finding.supporting_excerpt: We demonstrate with two specific tasks: (a) evaluating complex arithmetic expressions and (b) summarizing news articles. For both tasks, we create custom datasets to fine-tune an LLM.
finding.guard_note: relabelled ai_interpretation: a challenge is a judgement; its quoted excerpt was checked against the source

finding.claim: S4 is labelled a high-confidence verified fact, but 'fragmented' is the Science agent's own characterization. The survey abstract says it provides a systematic comparison across platforms. The Apple Silicon profiling paper and LLMCompass are not about the CPU/GPU/FPGA/ASIC/PIM taxonomy. The 'differing trade-offs' claim is therefore interpretation drawn from abstracts, not a quoted finding.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: The cited abstracts do not state that the literature is fragmented. The survey presents itself as unifying. The label and confidence should be downgraded.

finding.claim: S12 presents structural embedding projection as a lever on inference cost. The abstract reports quality results (perplexity, coherence) and only vague, dataset-dependent speed trade-offs, with no quantified latency or memory gain. It is one preprint with a loosely defined method, so it adds little to the inference-efficiency picture.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: Improved perplexity is not an inference-cost result. The abstract mentions 'variations across different datasets' without numbers. It should be treated as weak, not as an established trend.

finding.claim: S13's claim that co-design is 'the dominant strategy' generalizes from a hand-picked set of seven papers. Several other retrieved papers achieve gains without hardware pairing. Lookahead decoding is a purely algorithmic exact decoder, GEAR is KV-cache compression, and Splitwise/ShuffleInfer are scheduling changes. The memory-bandwidth-bound structure of decoding also suggests that hardware or system fixes are often unavoidable, not a chosen design philosophy. The pattern may reflect the search selection, not the field.
finding.label: ai_interpretation
finding.rationale: A 'dominant' claim needs a representative sample, and none is given. Counter-examples are in the evidence set, and abstracts alone cannot establish how common co-design is.

limitations: Only 12 papers were reviewed, and only their titles and abstracts (text_depth: abstract_only). Methods, baselines, error bars and limitations sections were not read.
Many sources are arXiv or Zenodo preprints that are not peer reviewed, including GEAR, Pie, CIMERA, WattGPU, TokenPowerBench and the HBM paper.

No paper in this set covers security, privacy, reliability or failure rates at scale, cost per token in real deployments, or competing approaches such as smaller models or non-GPU accelerators beyond the benchmarking paper. These are gaps in the retrieved evidence, not evidence of absence.
Retrieval covered mostly systems and architecture papers, so economic, regulatory and demand-side risks are not addressed.
Some abstracts are truncated (TokenPowerBench, WattGPU, the survey), so the full claims may be missing.
The 2026 publication dates cannot be verified here and no conclusions about market timing are drawn.
Only titles and abstracts were reviewed. Several abstracts are truncated (FlightLLM batch conditions, Apple Silicon results), so some caveats may be addressed in full texts.
Most evidence is preprints with self-reported results. Peer review and independent replication were not assessed.

The evidence set is small (24 papers), so I could not check whether other literature contradicts findings such as S9 to S11. I left S1, S2, S9, S10 and S11 unchallenged because their abstracts support them as stated, with appropriate hedging in S10.
Some retrieved papers carry future-dated metadata (2026), which may indicate unreliable dates. This was not investigated.

draft.summary: Evidence for large language model inference is unusually broad: research output on the exact phrase grew from 59 works in 2024 to 132 in 2025 and 411 in a partial 2026 (123.7% reported 2024->2025 acceleration), and patent publications grew 110->231 in the same step, with an unquantified application pool (S4, P1-P5). Activity is concentrated in two places: hardware acceleration across GPU, FPGA, ASIC and near-memory platforms with increasingly inference-specific memory (HBM) and packaging, and software or algorithmic tricks (early exit, sparsity, quantization, scheduling, custom kernels) that mostly only deliver gains when paired with hardware or kernel changes (S1-S13, M1-M9, P1-P4). Company filings show real money moving — AMD's ~$2.9bn agreement to acquire Taalas, Intel's Crescent Island, Qualcomm's High Bandwidth Compute, Micron's HBM-centred data centre business, Marvell packaging and Lam HBM stacking equipment — but none of the findings quantify inference revenue, customers or units (M1-M9). The main unresolved problem is structural: decoding is memory-bandwidth bound (R2), energy availability is described as the largest constraint on data centre expansion (R1), and HBM plus advanced packaging are argued to be potential single points of failure (R3). HBM supply is described in social posts as sold out through 2027 (X4, unverified), and all five related stocks carry high recent volatility even after steep drawdowns (T1-T11), so the dominant uncertainty is whether supply, power and measured-efficiency claims hold up rather than whether demand exists.
draft.plain_summary: Large language model inference is the computing work of getting an already-trained AI model to answer questions, and it is the part of AI that runs constantly and consumes most of the electricity. The evidence says the field is genuinely busy: scientific papers, patent filings and company spending on special chips and memory are all rising fast, and several chip and memory makers are selling products aimed at it. The thing most likely to slow it down is not demand but limits — the memory and power needed to serve these models may not be available fast enough, and many of the claimed speed-ups are still small tests by the people who built them.

themes.name: Inference software and algorithmic acceleration
technologies: custom CUDA kernels and embedding-stage changes

horizons.label: ai_interpretation
horizons.assessment: The work is early-stage and mostly self-reported: several results are on small or narrow settings (Pythia 70M-2.8B models in C4; two tasks in C5) and measured energy gains of up to 73% are explicitly conditional on matching optimizations to workload (S10). Patent filings do show scheduling, load balancing, token pruning and reasoning-fusion applications (P2, P3) and social posts show serving-stack activity such as Google's XLA Serving Engine optimised on Arm and a $1.3bn raise by inference startup Fal (X7, unverified), but no finding quantifies commercial deployment.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Co-design is repeatedly observed — algorithmic changes paired with kernels, DSP chains or NPU/CPU partitioning (S13, S1, S2, S7, S8) — but C8 argues this pattern may reflect search selection rather than the field, since lookahead decoding, KV-cache compression and scheduling changes deliver gains without hardware pairing. Whether these techniques hold at frontier scale and in batched serving is not shown (C3, C4).

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: The findings say nothing about whether algorithmic acceleration produces durable commercial advantage; optimizing compilers frameworks and serving stacks are not covered by financial or customer evidence here. Any long-run view would rest on the structural memory-bandwidth bottleneck being softened (R2, S6), which the evidence shows is only partly addressed.

bull.label: forecast
bull.narrative: There is a wide, active set of levers beyond raw silicon: GPU decoding bottlenecks addressed by asynchronous softmax and flat-GEMM buffering (S1), self-supervised early-exit heads that beat manually tuned baselines with little tuning (S7), self-selected attention spans converted into sparse masks with a custom kernel (S8), adaptive computation (S6), quantized and compressed models on FPGA and smartphone-class hardware (S2, S3), and reported up-to-73% energy reductions when optimizations are matched to the workload (S10). Patent filings map onto the same ground — dynamic load balancing, token-boundary scheduling and cloud-to-edge offloading (P2) and token pruning, attention-state adaptation and reasoning fusion (P3) — with the applicant pool spread across packaging firms, AI chip startups, cloud/tech enterprises and universities (P4).

base.label: ai_interpretation
base.narrative: The techniques work in their own settings but the evidence does not support general claims. Per-token dynamism can create synchronization bottlenecks and reduce throughput in batched inference (S6, though C3 notes this rests largely on one source), KV-cache compression trades quality for memory with errors compounding across autoregressive steps and 'near-lossless' being self-reported (R4), several optimizations depend on specific hardware or fast interconnects (R6), and headline gains come from incomparable baselines (R5). Quantization is explicitly not universally a speed win, with dequantization overhead among bottlenecks (S11).

bear.label: ai_interpretation
bear.narrative: The advertised gains are narrower than they appear. The self-supervised early-exit result comes only from 70M-2.8B Pythia models and the 1.66x is higher token acceptance relative to LayerSkip, not measured end-to-end speedup (C4); the self-selected attention span shows 28% throughput gain on two tasks with custom datasets and task-specific fine-tuning (C5); structural embedding projection reports only vague, dataset-dependent speed trade-offs with no quantified latency or memory gain and is a single preprint (S12, C7). If the memory-bandwidth-bound structure of decoding makes hardware or system fixes unavoidable (C8, R2), purely algorithmic acceleration has a limited ceiling.

horizons.label: ai_interpretation
horizons.assessment: Evidence is thin: one smartphone-class serving result beyond memory capacity (S2), one filing on edge-case handling with a dedicated inference system (P4), and one filing on offloading large edge model tasks (P2). Company evidence is product description only — Qualcomm's Hexagon NPU for on-device inference (M3) and AMD's 2025 Radeon AI PRO launch for local AI inference and professional workstations (M6). No finding quantifies unit sales or adoption.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: The findings support the plausibility of running compressed models locally — FPGA mapping of compressed LLMs (S3) and neuron-cluster decomposition split across NPU and CPU (S2) — but S3's advantage is challenged as being against an older GPU on one model (C1), and quantization is shown not to be a universal speed win across Apple M-series and NVIDIA GPUs (S11). No evidence covers cost, battery or commercial terms for edge deployment.

horizons.label: forecast
horizons.assessment: Nothing in the findings addresses the long-run economics of on-device inference, including whether local execution substitutes for cloud serving or complements it. Large unified memory is reported to favour Apple Silicon for very large models (S11), but this is a profiling observation, not a market forecast.

bull.label: forecast
bull.narrative: Serving models beyond device memory has been demonstrated by decomposing matrix operations into neuron clusters and splitting dense clusters to an NPU while sending sparse clusters to the CPU, pipelining I/O with computation (S2), and hardware-specific mapping flows exploit DSP chains and heterogeneous memory hierarchies to run compressed LLMs (S3). Vendors describe matching products: Qualcomm's Hexagon NPU for on-device inference alongside its data centre HBC work (M3) and AMD's 2025 Radeon AI PRO R9000 series for local AI inference and professional workstations (M6). Profiling suggests large unified memory can favour Apple Silicon for very large models (S11).

base.label: ai_interpretation
base.narrative: The capability is shown in research settings only. There is no finding on edge inference volumes, pricing, energy per query on a real device, or customers, and the only commercial statements are product descriptions in filings (M3, M6). Quantization — the usual enabler of edge deployment — is found not to promise faster inference on every platform, with dequantization overhead among the identified bottlenecks (S11).

bear.label: ai_interpretation
bear.narrative: The strongest edge-inference efficiency claim is contested: S3's FPGA energy and cost advantage is measured against an older NVIDIA V100S on LLaMA2-7B only, under a partially undisclosed batch setting, and is self-reported by the authors (C1). Embedding-stage modifications such as structural embedding projection report only dataset-dependent speed trade-offs with no quantified latency or memory gain and come from a single preprint (S12, C7). With no financial, unit or customer disclosure for edge inference anywhere in the findings, the commercial case is unverified.

This is not level 4-5 because there is genuine shipping product and no finding shows the approach failing or being blocked; it is not level 1-2 because the efficiency claims are mostly self-reported and incomparable (R5, C1-C8) and the memory and power constraints are unresolved.

missing_data: No customer-adoption evidence: no finding names a paying customer, deployment, unit volume, backlog or contract for any inference product or service.

No company evidence from the Company Scout agent: no K1 findings were produced, so there is no code-computed next-runner list, no SEC financials for the smaller patent assignees, and no mapping of patent assignees to listed companies. The patent assignees named as non-SEC-listed (e.g. 주식회사 인텔렉처퓨처아이피매니지먼트, 아이이엔건축사사무소주식회사, 江苏极目行远科技有限公司, 四川矽容微电子科技有限公司, 上海全境智宇科技有限公司, 주식회사 디노티시아) have no financial or business information attached.
No revenue, margin, unit-economics or pricing evidence for inference silicon, HBM or inference software in any finding.

No independent, third-party benchmarking of the efficiency claims: all S-findings' speedups and energy figures are from the authors' own abstracts, and C1-C8 show several are narrow, simulated-only or measured against older hardware.
No data on the actual share of AI power consumed by inference; the >90% figure is attributed to unnamed industry reports (R8).
No detail from the Market agent on customer contracts or demand beyond company descriptions; filings quoted here describe products and demand expectations, not bookings.
No quantitative evidence on on-device or edge inference commercial traction despite product descriptions (M3, M6).
limitations: All Science findings are abstract-level: the underlying papers were not read in full, so methods, baselines and generalisation are judged from truncated text, as C1-C8 repeatedly show.

Several public-company signals come from social posts (X1-X7) by company, standards-body and press accounts; they are unverified claims and are used only as context or catalysts, not as the basis of any rating.

The research and patent counts use exact-phrase or classifier matching, are not normalised for overall growth in publishing or filing, and the current year is partial; 2026 patent counts are explicitly likely undercounts (P5).

No Company Scout findings (K1) were produced, so smaller listed companies active on the topic, their financials and the next-runner heuristic are absent; the company list here comes only from Market filings and social posts.
Market findings are short filing excerpts and headlines; a filing describing a product is not evidence of sales, and no headline-based claim is treated as fact.
Price and timing findings (T1-T11) are code-computed over roughly 100 trading days and are risk context only; they are not used as entry points, timing signals or price expectations.
This is a research assessment over a 1-5 year horizon, not investment advice, and it contains no price targets, recommendations or expected returns.

dimensions.label: Research Momentum
dimensions.rationale: OpenAlex works containing the exact phrase grew 11 (2023) -> 59 (2024) -> 132 (2025, +123.7% YoY) with 411 in the partial 2026 against 85 at the same point in 2025 (+348.2%), and the retrieved literature spans GPU, FPGA, smartphone, Apple Silicon, energy and scheduling work (S1-S13). The exact-phrase method excludes synonyms and is not normalised for overall publishing growth, so the level is indicative rather than exact.

dimensions.label: Patent Momentum
dimensions.rationale: Patent publications rose 63 (2022) to 75 to 110 to 231 (2025, +110% YoY) with 382 counted in 2026, and filings concentrate on HBM/3D stacking/error correction (P1) as well as scheduling, pruning and fusion (P2, P3) across a fragmented applicant pool including Korean, Chinese, semiconductor packaging, chip-startup, cloud and academic filers (P4). The 2026 figure is likely an undercount from publication delay (P5), which lowers confidence in the level but not the direction.

dimensions.label: Technical Feasibility
dimensions.rationale: Techniques are demonstrated across platforms (S1, S2, S3, S7, S8) but the challenges show narrow validation: small Pythia models for early exit (C4), two tasks for sparse attention (C5), a single disputed FPGA-versus-old-GPU comparison (C1), and simulated-only hardware gains (C2). Feasible in principle, not proven at production scale.

dimensions.label: Commercial Readiness
dimensions.rationale: Named products exist — AMD's Radeon AI PRO R9000 launched in 2025 for local AI inference (M6), Intel's Crescent Island engineered for data centre inference (M2), Qualcomm's HBC architecture (M3), Micron's HBM-centred data centre business (M4) — and AMD agreed to pay ~$2.9bn for inference-silicon developer Taalas (M1). But these are company descriptions and transactions, not evidence of volume production economics, yield or pricing for inference specifically, and the literature notes design tools and power-measurement methods remain immature (S5, R7).

dimensions.label: Industry Investment
dimensions.rationale: Investment is large and visible: AMD agreed to acquire Taalas for approximately $2.9bn in cash and stock including up to ~$1.4bn contingent consideration (M1), and AMD, Intel, Qualcomm, Micron, Marvell and Lam Research all describe inference workloads or HBM in their filings (M9, M2-M8). A social post reports a $1.3bn raise by inference startup Fal (X7, unverified) — a headline-level claim given little weight.

dimensions.label: Competitive Position
dimensions.rationale: The evidence points to a fragmented, contested field rather than a defendable position: the acceleration literature spans CPU, GPU, FPGA, ASIC and PIM/NDP with differing trade-offs (S4, though C6 notes 'fragmented' is the agent's own characterisation) and the patent applicant pool mixes packaging firms, AI chip startups, cloud/tech enterprises and universities with notable Korean and Chinese activity (P4). No finding identifies a leader.

dimensions.label: Supply-Chain Readiness
dimensions.rationale: Supply-chain elements exist — Micron HBM for all data centre customers (M4), Marvell custom HBM and packaging (M7), Lam 3D HBM stacking equipment (M8) — but the findings describe constraints and fragility rather than readiness: HBM and advanced packaging are argued to be potential single points of failure (R3), energy availability is described as the largest constraint on data centre expansion (R1), and social posts claim HBM is sold out through 2027 with demand growth outpacing supply (X4, unverified).

notes: Weights are initial assumptions, not fitted to data. The score is an explainable heuristic, not a validated prediction of stock performance.
Sources are de-duplicated by URL/DOI/title. A single announcement reported by several outlets is not yet merged into one event.
Confidence lowered to 'medium': coverage is 90%, but the cited ratings themselves are mostly of lower confidence.
score.formula: base = sum(weight x rating/5) / sum(weight of evidenced dimensions) x 100; score = base x (1 - max_penalty x risk_rating/5). Dimensions without cited findings are 'missing', not zero.
